title: Archaeologists Just Found a Fascinating Ancient Statue—Used as a Paving Stone in a Roman Road - Nautilus
gist: Archaeologists at the Sardis site in western Turkey found a 2,500-year-old Lydian marble statue that had been halved and reused face-down as paving in a Roman road, offering clues to the period and to Roman disregard for Lydian art.

insights.claim: A 2,500-year-old marble statue from the Lydia kingdom was discovered at the Sardis site in western Turkey, halved and placed face-down along a major Roman colonnaded avenue.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: A concrete archaeological find offering clues about Lydian culture and its later treatment.
insights.locator: a mysterious 2,500-year-old marble statue that archaeologists working at the Sardis site

insights.claim: The original was a roughly 7-foot statue of a prominent Lydian figure, later broken up and recycled as paving slabs.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Underscores the stature of the subject and the indignity of the reuse.
insights.locator: an artist sculpted a 7-foot statue of you

insights.claim: The Romans arrived in Sardis in 133 BCE and apparently were not reverential toward Lydian art and sculpture, repurposing the statue as road material.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: The reuse offers a window into how conquering cultures treated the artifacts of those they absorbed.
insights.locator: The Romans arrived in Sardis in 133 BCE
